author: hoeschec
text:
Two great opportunities to buy. Notice the green lines prior to each trade... the line sets up a demand zone which is taken out.

If you are looking to take a long trade, look for a false demand zone. If you are looking to take a short trade, look for a false supply zone. Often, these 'false' zones form just above or below an important high time frame area (target). In older posts, I talk about magnetic attraction (a concept Salivan has also mentioned).

Price is drawn to origins and important FL's at swap zones because they contain large amounts of orders. When price comes really close to one of these zones of magnetic attraction, but fails to actually hit the zone, we have a possible 'false' zone setting up.

author: hoeschec
text:
Referring back to Post # 2349:

Here is a re-post of the chart I made:

My philosophy is an off-shoot of the main concepts taught here on RTM. Several weeks ago I began a study in to understanding why price bounces and fakes out. If you remember back to my old posts for 2016/2017 you will see I focused almost exclusively on trading the return to a fakeout that already occurred in the past. That is still a good strategy & approach to trading the market, but I always wondered how difficult it would be to trade the FO as is occurred instead of trading the return to the FO.

Trading the FO as it forms has its own benefits: mainly better RR and quick trades. Also, it's REALLY fun!

I've noticed that traders tend to form their own strategies over time as they gravitate towards a certain 'type' of trading style or methodology.

I strongly believe that price moves because of order flow. Price moves in the direction of liquidity. It is always bouncing around as the war between bears and bulls rages on. Finding where the true or 'free' or 'fresh' order flow exists is key to knowing which direction price is headed. As I mentioned yesterday, I believe true order flow exists in the tiny FL formed when price engulfs an important levels (ORFL, SWAP, FL's etc...).

Most traders on RTM know how to draw the FL boxes. They are fun to draw, and they do an excellent job of framing the market in a visual structure that draws our eyes towards the important decisions and the relevant areas of order flow.

Lately, I have been studying how to draw the FL Boxes properly. Often times, price will engulf a level and form a new FL on a LTF but price will form multiple iterations as it passes above and below that initial FL to form a HTF FL. I've heard others refer to this as an 'inner' FL and an 'outer' FL.

In my opinion (and I admit i'm still learning as I explore chart after chart after chart...) the first engulf and FL formed after price breaks an important level is the most important FL in terms of order flow. The HTF FL's that form outside of the inner FL is like a 'shell' and it's important too... but not as important the tiny inner FL.

This distinction of the inner vs outer FL is very important because we draw the boxes based on engulfs of previous boxes. Once these start getting drawn in multiple scales (fractals) we see a type of divergence or "deviation" exists between the fractals. This divergence/deviation looks like a gap of space where the distal boundaries of one FL (in one TF) are different from the distal boundaries of another FL (in a different TF). Why does this matter to us? Because if we are looking on the higher TF scale we might expect price to bounce in a particular FL where this gap exists...and price will overrun the FL making it look like price engulfed in the wrong direction when in reality it was just bouncing from the lower scale FL. Usually, these Lower scale FL's are accompanied by a false supply/demand level to create a bear/bull trap as well.

Since each new FL box depend on engulfs of preceding FL boxes, finding the exact starting point is CRITICAL. If the first FL box is incorrectly drawn, or is based on an engulf of a wrong level (or an engulf of the wrong scale) the proceeding boxes will all be wrong. Identifying the right starting point is my main focus right now...this is what I am currently working on. I will post more info when I find good examples to share.

I know this is a really hard concept to explain using words... hopefully I can find some good examples to post in my next few posts. I am still figuring this out as I go too. I am feeling highly motivated and I am excited to find out where these new discoveries will lead. Hopefully, if I am on the right track (and I think I am), I can post this information on my journal to help others as well!

Some quick thoughts on EUR-JPY:

Following the pro money:

Box 1 is important because it is the location of bull stops from the FO bull trap above (yellow circle).

Look at the red circle and you will see where the buy orders are. Box # 2 is just a distraction that attracts traders who buy too soon. These early Buyers get stopped out when price breaks the low of Box 2.

This is the ideal approach to an area of interest: If the spot you want to buy/sell is legitimately important, chances are there will be some kind of a trap leading into that zone to shake out traders who either don't understand what's happening or have their SL too tight.

author: hoeschec
text:
Here is a trade I took on GU with the help of a friend:

I recently closed it out... the methodology is more or less the same:

Find a FL that can be broken, in to an area of LQ that remains somewhat hidden or obscured in some way. Consider what professional money/institutional money must to to adequately fill their orders. If pro money needs to BUY they need lots of LQ from those willing to SELL

If it looks like price is going up, nobody is going to be willing to sell...so... we look for evidence that professional money is active by looking for these tricky spots that trap LQ.
